grammar.title: Past modals
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Needn't have + pp** x **didn't need to + verbo**
- **needn't have done** = você **fez**, mas **não era necessário** (esforço desperdiçado):
"You **needn't have brought** a cake — we already had three!" (você trouxe, mas não precisava)
- **didn't need to do** = **não era necessário** (geralmente a pessoa **não fez**):
"I **didn't need to** take a taxi because Ana gave me a lift."

**2. Should have / Ought to have + pp** → crítica ou arrependimento (o certo não aconteceu)
- "You **should have told** me!" / "I **ought to have checked** the date."
- Negativa: "I **shouldn't have eaten** so much."

**3. Could have + pp** → possibilidade que **não aconteceu**, ou crítica
- "You **could have been** killed!" (podia ter acontecido)
- "You **could have called**!" (crítica: você podia ter ligado — e não ligou)
- **Couldn't have + pp** = impossível no passado: "I **couldn't have done** it without you."

**4. Might have / May have + pp** → especulação sobre o passado (talvez)
- "She **might have missed** the bus." / "It **may have been** a mistake."
- "It **might have been** worse." (poderia ter sido pior)

**5. Would have + pp** → disposição/vontade no passado (ligado a condições)
- "I **would have helped** you, but you didn't ask."
- "I **wouldn't have** done that." (eu, no seu lugar, não teria feito)

**6. Revisão B1+:** **must have** (dedução: certeza) · **can't have** (impossível).

**Na fala:** should've = "**shúdav**", could've = "**kúdav**", needn't have = "**nídentav**".

rows: You needn't have cooked — we ate out.
I didn't need to wait; the bus came.
I would have come, but I was ill.
She must have left. / He can't have known.

examples.en: I spent the whole night preparing for the interview, but I needn't have worried — they offered me the job in ten minutes.
examples.pt: Passei a noite toda me preparando para a entrevista, mas não precisava ter me preocupado — me ofereceram o emprego em dez minutos.

grammar.tip_pt: Em português, "podia ter" serve para tudo. Em inglês, escolha: **could have** (era possível), **should have** (era o certo), **might have** (talvez tenha acontecido).

pronunciation.focus: Formas reduzidas: should've, could've, needn't have
pronunciation.tip_pt: Nativos reduzem o **have** a um "av" fraco, colado no modal: **should've** "shúdav", **could've** "kúdav", **might've** "máitav", **needn't have** "nídentav". ⚠️ Na escrita, nunca escreva "should of" — é um erro comum até entre nativos, por causa da pronúncia.

listening.title: The worry experiment
listening.context_pt: Um psicólogo fala num podcast sobre preocupações que nunca se concretizam.

lines.speaker: Psychologist
lines.en: Here's an exercise I often suggest. For two weeks, write down every worry you have — "I might lose my job", "My presentation will be a disaster" — and then check later whether it actually happened. In a small study at Penn State University, researchers asked people with generalized anxiety to do something similar. They found that most of the participants' worries did not come true, and when something negative did happen, people often coped better than they had expected. In other words, they needn't have worried so much. Of course, this doesn't mean all worry is useless. Some concern helps us prepare. But if you look back at your list and see that you spent hours worrying about things that never happened, it can be a real wake-up call. You might decide to save your energy for the problems that actually appear.

questions.q: What exercise does the psychologist suggest?
questions.answer: Writing down every worry for two weeks and checking later whether it happened.

questions.answer: Most worries did not come true, and people coped better than expected.

reading.title: Lucky breaks
reading.text: History is full of people whose failures turned out to be blessings in disguise. Take the author J.K. Rowling, who has said in interviews that her manuscript for the first Harry Potter book was rejected by many publishers before Bloomsbury accepted it. Any one of those editors could have changed literary history; they simply didn't. Steve Jobs, forced out of Apple in 1985, later described being fired as one of the best things that could have happened to him, because it freed him to start again. Of course, survivor stories like these can be misleading. For every person whose rejection led to success, there are many others who might have been equally talented but never got a second chance. Psychologist Richard Wiseman, who studied people who considered themselves lucky or unlucky, suggested that "lucky" people tend to notice opportunities, listen to their intuition and recover quickly from bad experiences. In one of his well-known experiments, participants were asked to count the photographs in a newspaper. Many of the "unlucky" ones missed a large message inside it telling them they needn't have kept counting. Perhaps luck is partly a matter of where we choose to look.

writing.model:
The best mistake I ever made

Three years ago, I sent an email that I definitely shouldn't have sent. I was working in a marketing agency, and after a terrible meeting I wrote a long message complaining about our biggest client. I meant to send it to my best friend. Instead, I sent it to my boss.

I should have read the address twice. I could have waited until I was calmer. I certainly needn't have used so many capital letters! My heart stopped when I realized what I'd done. I was sure I would be fired — and honestly, many bosses would have fired me on the spot.

But my boss called me into her office and, to my surprise, she said she agreed with most of my points. She'd been thinking the same about that client for months. She might have been annoyed by my tone, but she said I'd shown that I really cared about the quality of our work.

Two weeks later, she asked me to lead a new project to improve how we managed difficult clients. Within a year, I'd been promoted.

Looking back, it could have ended very badly. I was lucky, and I don't recommend sending angry emails! But the mistake taught me something important: sometimes being honest — in the right way — can open doors. These days, though, I always check the address.

culture_note.title: "Should of"?

Se você escrever "should have", estará escrevendo melhor que muitos nativos!

warmup.text_pt: "Eu odeio **ser interrompido**." "Ela parece **ter esquecido**." "Ele nega **ter dito** isso." Para expressar ideias mais complexas, o inglês usa gerúndios e infinitivos **passivos** e **perfeitos**. Hoje você vai usá-los para falar sobre comunicação e como queremos ser tratados.

grammar.title: Advanced gerunds and infinitives
grammar.explanation_pt:
Você já sabe quais verbos pedem **-ing** (enjoy, avoid, deny, mind...) e quais pedem **to** (want, decide, seem, expect...). Agora vamos às formas **passivas** e **perfeitas**:

| | Gerúndio | Infinitivo |
|---|---|---|
| simples | doing | to do |
| **passivo** | **being done** | **to be done** |
| **perfeito** | **having done** | **to have done** |
| **perfeito passivo** | having been done | to have been done |

**1. Passivo** → o sujeito **recebe** a ação:
- "I hate **being interrupted**." (eu sou interrompido)
- "Nobody likes **being criticized** in public."
- "Everyone wants **to be taken** seriously."
- "The report needs **to be finished** today."

**2. Perfeito** → ação **anterior** ao verbo principal:
- "He denied **having taken** the money." (negou ter pegado)
- "She seems **to have forgotten** our meeting." (parece ter esquecido)
- "I regret **not having studied** more." (= I regret not studying more — também correto)
- "He's thought **to have left** the country." (formal)

**3. Verbos que mudam de sentido:**
- **remember / forget + -ing** = lembrar/esquecer de algo que **aconteceu** ("I remember **meeting** her.")
- **remember / forget + to** = lembrar/esquecer de **fazer** algo ("Remember **to call** her.")
- **stop + -ing** = parar uma atividade · **stop + to** = parar **para** fazer outra coisa
- **try + -ing** = experimentar ("Try **turning** it off and on.") · **try + to** = tentar com esforço ("I tried **to open** it, but I couldn't.")
- **regret + -ing** = arrepender-se · **regret + to** = lamentar informar (formal: "We regret **to inform** you...")

rows: Lembro de ter trancado a porta.

listening.title: The art of listening
listening.context_pt: Uma especialista em comunicação explica a escuta ativa.

lines.speaker: Speaker
lines.en: Most of us think we're good listeners. But research on communication suggests that we often listen in order to reply, not to understand. While the other person is talking, we're planning what to say next. Active listening is different. It means giving the person your full attention, avoiding being distracted by your phone, and trying not to interrupt. It also means checking that you've understood: "So what you're saying is..." People who are listened to in this way feel respected. They're more likely to trust you, and less likely to feel misunderstood. A simple exercise: in your next conversation, try waiting two seconds before you reply. You'll be surprised how much more you notice — including what's said between the lines.

questions.q: How do people feel when they are listened to this way?

reading.title: Why we want to be understood
reading.text: Being understood is one of our deepest psychological needs. Researchers studying relationships have found that people who feel understood by their partners tend to report higher satisfaction, and in some studies even smaller increases in stress during conflict. Interestingly, it seems that what matters most is not having our ideas accepted, but being listened to. In one line of research, participants who were allowed to explain their point of view — even when the other person disagreed — reported feeling more respected than those who were simply agreed with quickly. Feeling misunderstood, on the other hand, can be painful. Many people describe being left out or not being taken seriously at work as one of the most frustrating experiences of their professional lives. Psychologists suggest a few habits for helping others feel understood: asking open questions, repeating key points in your own words and avoiding being too quick to give advice. Admitting to having made assumptions also helps: "I think I misunderstood you — can you explain again?" Sometimes, the most powerful thing we can do is not to have the right answer, but to have truly listened.

questions.q: What have researchers found about people who feel understood by their partners?
questions.answer: They tend to report higher satisfaction (and sometimes less stress during conflict).

questions.q: What matters most, according to the text?
questions.answer: Being listened to, not having our ideas accepted.

questions.q: What is one of the most frustrating experiences at work for many people?

questions.q: Name two habits that help others feel understood.
questions.answer: Asking open questions / repeating key points / not giving advice too quickly / admitting assumptions.

writing.task: Write a short article (200–240 words) for a company newsletter titled "How to make your colleagues feel heard". Use at least 6 passive or perfect gerunds/infinitives and 2 verbs that change meaning (remember, stop, try).
writing.task_pt: Escreva um artigo curto (200–240 palavras) para o boletim de uma empresa intitulado "Como fazer seus colegas se sentirem ouvidos". Use pelo menos 6 gerúndios/infinitivos passivos ou perfeitos e 2 verbos que mudam de sentido (remember, stop, try).
writing.model:
How to make your colleagues feel heard

In our last staff survey, many of you said that you wanted to be listened to more in meetings. Nobody likes being interrupted or having their ideas ignored. Here are four simple habits that can help.

1. Stop multitasking. When a colleague is speaking, try putting your phone face down. Being given someone's full attention is rare these days — and people notice it.

2. Let people finish. Many of us interrupt without realizing it. If you remember interrupting someone, go back to them: "Sorry, I cut you off — please continue."

3. Give credit. Nothing is more frustrating than seeing your idea presented by someone else. If you build on a colleague's idea, mention them. Everyone deserves to be recognized for their contributions.

4. Check your understanding. Before you reply, try repeating the main point in your own words. If you realize you've misunderstood, admit having made an assumption. It shows respect.

These habits take practice. Several team leaders who tested them last month said they were surprised to have noticed so many changes in their meetings. One said: "People seem to have become more confident about sharing ideas."

Next time you're in a meeting, remember to listen as carefully as you'd like to be listened to.

culture_note.title: Comunicação direta x indireta
culture_note.text_pt: Culturas variam no nível de **franqueza**. Holandeses e alemães são conhecidos por feedback direto; britânicos, por indiretas ("**That's an interesting idea**" pode significar "não gostei"). Brasileiros costumam suavizar críticas e valorizar a relação. Em equipes internacionais, **read between the lines** — e, se não tiver certeza, pergunte.

summary_pt: Passivo: being told / to be taken.

grammar.title: Collocations and idioms
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Collocations com verbos "leves"**
- **make** (criar, produzir, resultado): make a mistake, a decision, a plan, a complaint, an effort, progress, money, friends, a difference, an excuse, a phone call
- **do** (tarefas, trabalho, atividades): do homework, the housework, research, business, a course, your best, a favour, damage, exercise
- **take** (ações, oportunidades): take a break, a risk, a photo, an exam, part in, place, advantage of, responsibility for, care of
- **have** (experiências, refeições): have a look, a chat, a good time, an argument, a shower, lunch, a go
- **pay** (dar algo): pay attention, a visit, a compliment, the price

**2. Adjetivo + substantivo** ("forte" muda em inglês!):
- **heavy** rain / traffic / smoker · **strong** coffee / wind / accent · **high** temperature / price / risk · **deep** sleep / concern · **bitter** disappointment · **close** friend · **broad** smile

**3. Advérbio + adjetivo** (intensificadores naturais):
- **highly** recommended / unlikely / successful · **deeply** grateful / concerned · **bitterly** disappointed / cold · **fully** aware · **completely** different · **perfectly** normal

**4. Idioms (expressões idiomáticas)**
- Use com moderação — idioms demais soam forçados.
- Muitos são **parecidos** com o português (break the ice = quebrar o gelo), mas outros **não**: "it's raining cats and dogs" ≈ "está chovendo canivetes"; "cost an arm and a leg" ≈ "custar os olhos da cara".
- Idioms são **fixos**: não troque palavras (❌ "a piece of pie").

**Estratégia:** ao aprender uma palavra nova, anote **com o que ela combina**, não só a tradução.

rows: a mistake, a decision, progress, an effort, a difference, money
homework, research, your best, a favour, business, exercise
a break, a risk, part in, place, advantage of, care of
a look, a chat, an argument, a go, fun

grammar.tip_pt: Os erros de collocation mais comuns de brasileiros: ❌ "do a mistake" (✅ make), ❌ "make a question" (✅ **ask** a question), ❌ "take a decision" (✅ **make** — embora "take" seja aceito no inglês britânico), ❌ "strong rain" (✅ heavy rain), ❌ "lose the bus" (✅ **miss** the bus).

pronunciation.tip_pt: Collocations e idioms são pronunciados como **um bloco só**, com as palavras ligadas: "make a mistake" = "mêikamistêik", "take a break" = "têikabrêik", "a piece of cake" = "apísovkêik". Aprender em blocos melhora a **fluência** e a **velocidade**.

listening.title: Idioms around the world
listening.context_pt: Um podcast compara expressões idiomáticas em diferentes línguas.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Today we're comparing idioms from different languages. Let's start with rain. In English, when it's raining heavily, people sometimes say "it's raining cats and dogs" — though, honestly, most people just say "it's pouring". In Brazilian Portuguese, it's "raining pocket knives".

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.en: I love that one! And when something is very expensive, English speakers say it "costs an arm and a leg", whereas Brazilians say it "costs the eyes of the face". Same idea — very valuable parts of the body!

lines.speaker: Host
lines.en: Exactly. And some idioms are almost identical. "Break the ice" exists in English, Portuguese and many other languages.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.en: My advice to learners: don't try to use too many idioms. Collocations are more important. If you say "make a decision" and "heavy traffic" correctly, you'll sound more natural than if you use five idioms in one sentence!

questions.q: What do most English speakers actually say when it's raining heavily?
questions.answer: "It's pouring."

questions.q: What is the Portuguese equivalent of "cost an arm and a leg"?
questions.answer: "Custar os olhos da cara" (cost the eyes of the face).

questions.q: Which idiom exists in many languages?
questions.answer: Break the ice.

questions.q: What is the guest's advice to learners?
questions.answer: Don't use too many idioms; collocations are more important.

reading.title: Chunks, not words
reading.text: For most of the twentieth century, language teaching focused on two things: grammar rules and individual words. But in the 1990s, the linguist Michael Lewis proposed what he called the "Lexical Approach". His central idea was simple but powerful: language is not made of grammar and words, but largely of "chunks" — groups of words that native speakers store and use as single units. Phrases like "by the way", "I'm not sure", "make a decision" or "as far as I know" are not built word by word each time we speak; they come ready-made. Corpus research — the study of very large collections of real texts — supports this view, showing that a large part of everyday language consists of recurring combinations. This helps explain why learners can know thousands of words and still sound unnatural: they combine words in ways that are grammatically correct but that native speakers simply don't use, like "do a decision" or "strong rain". It also explains why fluent speakers can talk so quickly: they don't need to build every sentence from scratch. For learners, the practical lesson is clear. When you meet a new word, don't just learn its translation. Notice the words around it, write down the whole chunk, and practise it until it comes out automatically.

questions.q: What did Michael Lewis propose?
questions.answer: The Lexical Approach: language is largely made of chunks.

questions.q: What does corpus research show?
questions.answer: A large part of everyday language consists of recurring combinations.

questions.q: Why can learners know many words and still sound unnatural?
questions.answer: They combine words in ways native speakers don't use.

questions.q: What is the practical lesson for learners?
questions.answer: Learn whole chunks, not just translations, and practise them.

writing.model:
Review: A weekend at Pousada Mar Azul, Ilhabela

I'd been working long hours for months, so I decided to take a break and spend a weekend on Ilhabela. A friend had highly recommended Pousada Mar Azul, and I'm deeply grateful she did.

The staff made a real effort to make us feel welcome. The owner, Dona Célia, paid us a visit on the first evening, broke the ice with some funny stories about the island and gave us excellent advice about where to go.

The rooms are simple but spotlessly clean, with a breathtaking view of the sea. On the second day there was heavy rain, but it turned out to be a blessing in disguise: we had a long chat with other guests in the lounge and made friends with a lovely couple from Chile.

Breakfast deserves a special mention. The coffee was strong, the fruit was fresh and the homemade cakes were absolutely delicious.

The only downside? Getting there. The ferry queue on a Friday afternoon can be extremely long, so pay attention to the timetable and arrive early.

It isn't cheap, but it certainly doesn't cost an arm and a leg either, especially compared with other places on the island. All in all, it's a perfect place to relax, and I'd have no hesitation in recommending it. Five stars.

culture_note.title: Idioms que confundem
culture_note.text_pt: Cuidado com idioms que **parecem** traduções mas não são: **"to pull someone's leg"** = zoar alguém (não "puxar o pé"); **"break a leg!"** = boa sorte (no teatro); **"it's not my cup of tea"** = não é a minha praia; **"once in a blue moon"** = muito raramente. E o português **"pagar mico"** seria **"to make a fool of yourself"**.

grammar.title: B2 review and exam strategies
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Revisão das grandes estruturas do B2:**
- **Narrativa:** past perfect continuous, would / used to, inversão ("Never have I...")
- **Futuro:** future continuous / perfect ("By 2030, I'll have finished...")
- **Passiva e reporting:** "It is believed that...", "He is said to be..."
- **Condicionais:** third, mixed, wish / if only, alternativas ao if
- **Orações:** relative clauses avançadas, participle clauses
- **Coesão:** although / despite / whereas / however, linkers formais
- **Modais no passado:** needn't have, should have, could have, might have
- **Gerúndio / infinitivo:** being told, having done, to have done
- **Léxico:** collocations e idioms

**Formato das provas:**

**Cambridge B2 First** — 4 partes:
- **Reading & Use of English** (1h15): gramática, vocabulário e leitura
- **Writing** (1h20): essay obrigatório + uma tarefa à escolha (artigo, e-mail/carta, relatório ou resenha)
- **Listening** (cerca de 40 min)
- **Speaking** (cerca de 14 min, **em dupla**): entrevista, comparação de fotos, tarefa colaborativa e discussão

**IELTS Speaking** (11–14 min, individual):
- **Part 1**: perguntas sobre você (casa, trabalho, hobbies)
- **Part 2**: fale **1–2 minutos** sobre um tema de um cartão (1 min para preparar)
- **Part 3**: discussão mais abstrata sobre o tema da Part 2
- Critérios: fluência e coerência, vocabulário, gramática e pronúncia. No IELTS, B2 corresponde aproximadamente às bandas 5.5–6.5.

**Estratégias para o speaking:**
1. **Ganhe tempo** com naturalidade: "That's an interesting question...", "Let me think..."
2. **Desenvolva** (elaborate): responda + motivo + exemplo. Nunca só "yes" ou "no".
3. **Parafraseie** quando faltar uma palavra: "It's a kind of... / It's something you use to..."
4. **Autocorrija-se** rapidamente: "I goed — sorry, I went..."  — isso mostra controle.
5. Na prova em dupla, **interaja**: "What do you think?", "I see your point, but..."
6. **Mostre variedade**: use estruturas do B2 de propósito (conditionals, passivas, relative clauses).

rows: That's a good question. / Let me think about that for a second.
I can't remember the word, but it's a kind of... / It's what you use to...
The main reason is... For example, ... That's why...
What do you think? / Would you agree? / I see your point, but...
Sorry, could you repeat the question? / Do you mean...?
So, all in all, I'd say... / To sum up, ...

examples.en: That's an interesting question. I've never really thought about it, but I'd say that technology has made us more connected and, at the same time, lonelier.
examples.pt: Que pergunta interessante. Nunca pensei muito nisso, mas eu diria que a tecnologia nos tornou mais conectados e, ao mesmo tempo, mais solitários.

examples.en: I can't remember the exact word, but it's a kind of tool you use to measure temperature.
examples.pt: Não lembro a palavra exata, mas é um tipo de ferramenta que você usa para medir temperatura.

examples.en: If I had known how useful English would be, I would have started studying much earlier.
examples.pt: Se eu soubesse o quanto o inglês seria útil, teria começado a estudar bem mais cedo.

grammar.tip_pt: Na prova oral, **o examinador avalia o seu inglês, não as suas ideias**. Você não precisa dizer algo brilhante — precisa dizer algo **claro, desenvolvido e com variedade**. Se não tiver opinião, invente uma!

common_mistakes.wrong: Examiner: Do you like reading? — Student: Yes.
common_mistakes.right: Yes, I do, especially novels. I usually read before bed, because it helps me relax.

common_mistakes.wrong: I don't know how to say this in English, so... (silêncio)
common_mistakes.right: I can't think of the word, but it's a kind of...

common_mistakes.wrong: Usar só estruturas simples para não errar.
common_mistakes.right: Arriscar estruturas do B2 (If I had..., It is said that..., Having...)
common_mistakes.why_pt: A variedade conta pontos — pequenos erros com estruturas complexas são aceitáveis.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Fluência não é falar rápido — é falar **sem pausas longas no lugar errado**. Faça pausas **entre** blocos de sentido (não no meio de um chunk), use **fillers** naturais (well, actually, I mean, you know) com moderação e ligue as palavras dentro de cada bloco.
practice: Well, | to be honest, | I've never really thought about it.
Actually, | I'd say that | it depends on the situation.
I mean, | if I had known, | I would have done it differently.

dialogue.title: Mock speaking test
dialogue.context_pt: Simulação da parte colaborativa da prova oral B2 First: dois candidatos discutem uma pergunta.

lines.speaker: Examiner
lines.en: Now, I'd like you to talk together about how people can improve their mental well-being. Here are some ideas: exercise, spending time in nature, using less social media, talking to friends and learning something new. You have two minutes.
lines.pt: Agora, gostaria que vocês conversassem sobre como as pessoas podem melhorar seu bem-estar mental. Aqui estão algumas ideias: exercício, tempo na natureza, usar menos redes sociais, conversar com amigos e aprender algo novo. Vocês têm dois minutos.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: Shall we start with exercise? I think it's one of the most effective options. It is often said that even a short walk can improve your mood. What do you think?
lines.pt: Vamos começar com exercício? Acho que é uma das opções mais eficazes. Diz-se com frequência que até uma caminhada curta pode melhorar o humor. O que você acha?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: I agree, although not everyone has time to go to the gym. Having said that, you don't need a gym — you could just walk to work.
lines.pt: Concordo, embora nem todo mundo tenha tempo de ir à academia. Dito isso, você não precisa de academia — poderia simplesmente ir a pé para o trabalho.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: That's a good point. What about social media? If I had spent less time on my phone last year, I think I would have been much less anxious.
lines.pt: Bom argumento. E as redes sociais? Se eu tivesse passado menos tempo no celular no ano passado, acho que teria ficado bem menos ansiosa.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Me too. But I wouldn't say it's all negative. It can also help you stay in touch with friends who live far away, which links to the next idea.
lines.pt: Eu também. Mas eu não diria que é tudo negativo. Também pode ajudar a manter contato com amigos que moram longe, o que se liga à próxima ideia.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: True. And learning something new? I'd say it's important because it gives you a sense of progress. Learning English has definitely done that for me!
lines.pt: Verdade. E aprender algo novo? Eu diria que é importante porque dá uma sensação de progresso. Aprender inglês com certeza fez isso por mim!

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.en: Ha, absolutely. So, if we had to choose the most important one, I'd go for talking to friends. What about you?
lines.pt: Ha, com certeza. Então, se tivéssemos que escolher a mais importante, eu ficaria com conversar com amigos. E você?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.en: I see your point, but I'd choose exercise, because it helps both your body and your mind. Shall we say both?
lines.pt: Entendo seu ponto, mas eu escolheria exercício, porque ajuda o corpo e a mente. Vamos dizer as duas?

listening.title: IELTS Part 2: a long turn
listening.context_pt: Um candidato responde a um cartão do IELTS Speaking Part 2: "Describe a skill you learned that has been useful to you."

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.en: OK, so I'd like to talk about a skill that has been incredibly useful to me, which is speaking English. I started learning it at school, but to be honest, I didn't take it very seriously back then. It wasn't until I was about twenty-five, having just been offered a job in an international company, that I realized how much I needed it. So I signed up for an evening course. At first, it was really challenging — I remember being terrified of speaking in class. But my teacher encouraged us to make mistakes, which made a huge difference. The skill has been useful in so many ways. At work, I now lead meetings with colleagues in four countries. I've also travelled a lot more, and I've made friends from all over the world. If I hadn't learned English, I wouldn't have the job I have today. Looking back, I wish I'd started taking it seriously much earlier — I needn't have waited until I was twenty-five!

questions.q: What skill does the candidate talk about?
questions.answer: Speaking English.

questions.q: When did the candidate realize they needed English?
questions.answer: At about 25, after being offered a job in an international company.

questions.q: What made a huge difference in class?
questions.answer: The teacher encouraged them to make mistakes.

questions.q: Find two B2 structures the candidate uses.

reading.title: What does B2 really mean?
reading.text: According to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), a B2 user is an "independent user" who can understand the main ideas of complex texts, interact with native speakers with a degree of fluency and spontaneity, and produce clear, detailed texts on a wide range of subjects. In practical terms, this is a significant milestone. Many universities around the world accept B2 as a minimum level of English for some courses, and many international employers consider it the point at which someone can work effectively in English. However, reaching B2 does not mean that you will understand everything. You may still struggle with fast speech, strong regional accents, jokes and cultural references. You will continue to make mistakes — but, crucially, they will rarely prevent communication, and you will often be able to notice and correct them yourself. Perhaps the most important change is psychological. At B2, English stops being only a subject that you study and becomes a tool that you use: to read the news, watch series without subtitles, follow a TED talk or argue your point in a meeting. From here, progress depends less on courses and more on exposure. The more you read, listen and speak, the closer you will get to C1 — and, more importantly, the richer your life in English will become.

questions.q: How does the CEFR describe a B2 user?
questions.answer: An independent user who understands complex texts, interacts with fluency and produces clear, detailed texts.

questions.q: Why is B2 a significant milestone?
questions.answer: Many universities and employers accept it as a minimum level.

questions.q: What might you still struggle with at B2?
questions.answer: Fast speech, strong accents, jokes and cultural references.

questions.q: What does progress depend on after B2?
questions.answer: More on exposure (reading, listening, speaking) than on courses.

items.prompt: What's the best way to learn a language?
items.answer: Model: In my opinion, the best way is through exposure. If I hadn't started watching series in English, my listening wouldn't be so good. Classes are important, but you need to use the language every day.

writing.task: Write a B2 First–style essay (140–190 words): "Some people believe that with translation apps and AI, learning foreign languages is no longer necessary. Do you agree?" Write about 1) communication and relationships, 2) work and careers, and 3) your own idea. Show a wide range of B2 structures.
writing.task_pt: Escreva uma redação no estilo B2 First (140–190 palavras): "Algumas pessoas acreditam que, com apps de tradução e IA, aprender línguas estrangeiras não é mais necessário. Você concorda?" Escreva sobre 1) comunicação e relacionamentos, 2) trabalho e carreira e 3) uma ideia sua. Mostre variedade de estruturas do B2.
writing.model:
Is learning languages still necessary?

Translation apps have improved enormously in recent years. As a result, it could be argued that learning a foreign language is no longer worth the effort. However, I believe this view is mistaken.

Firstly, language is not only about exchanging information but also about building relationships. Although an app can translate words, it cannot easily capture humour, emotion or cultural references. Having made friends abroad, I know that real connection happens when you speak someone's language.

Secondly, in the job market, speaking English is still seen as an essential skill. Employers want people who can lead meetings and negotiate, which is extremely difficult to do through an app.

Finally, learning a language changes the way we think. It is widely believed that bilingual people are more flexible and open to other cultures.

In conclusion, while translation technology is a useful tool, it is not a substitute for learning. If I had relied on apps, I would never have had the experiences that English has given me.

culture_note.title: Depois do B2
culture_note.text_pt: O próximo passo é o **C1 (Advanced)**. Para chegar lá, o segredo é a **exposição**: leia notícias (BBC, The Guardian), ouça podcasts, assista séries e palestras sem legenda (ou com legenda em inglês) e **fale** sempre que puder. Se quiser certificar seu nível, pesquise as provas **Cambridge B2 First**, **IELTS** e **TOEFL** — cada uma tem formato e reconhecimento diferentes. Congratulations — and keep going!
